newsitem.title: ITALY: Priebke lawyer calls for trial to leave Rome.
newsitem.headline: Priebke lawyer calls for trial to leave Rome.

text.p: A lawyer representing former SS captain Erich Priebke said on Wednesday that a fresh war crimes trial ordered by Italy's appeal court should be moved out of Rome to ensure a fair hearing.

Lawyer Velio di Rezze said he would ask for the re-trial to be held in the northern cities of Turin or Verona because judges in Rome would "not be able to decide in peace, given what happened on the night of the last sentence."

Priebke first went on trial in a blaze of publicity on May 8, accused of complicity in the SS reprisal execution of 335 men and boys in the Ardeatine caves south of Rome in 1944. The massacre was Italy's worst World War Two atrocity.
The chaotic trial, at times bordering on farce, ended in a 2-1 verdict on August 1 to release the 83-year-old German.

The convoluted ruling drew swift condemnation from around the world and Priebke was besieged inside the courthouse by angry protesters. He was re-arrested hours later when Germany said it intended to extradite him for a trial there.
The Court of Cassation on Tuesday annulled the original controversial verdict and ordered that Priebke, who is being held in a Rome jail, should face a fresh trial.

The court did not rule on the verdict itself, but instead overturned a lower appeal court's decision dating from July which had rejected accusations that military judge Agostino Quistelli was biased in favour of the accused.
No date has yet been set for the fresh trial although military prosecutor Antonino Intelisano said that he expected it to open in mid-December.
He said that Rome remained the obvious place for the trial and suggested a fortified bunker in Rebibbia prison.
Di Rezze said Priebke, who has admitted shooting two people and checking off names from a list at the caves, was tired and sick and in danger of physical collapse.
"But he is ready for a new battle because he is still convinced he was only obeying orders," he said.
Quistelli said earlier that he had no regrets about his handling of the case despite the appeal court decision.
He had headed the panel of three judges which found Priebke guilty of multiple murder, but freed him because of mitigating circumstances and a statute of limitations.
"I wouldn't change a comma of what I did," Quistelli told La Repubblica newspaper in an interview.
"I tried an old man who represents no danger to society, who committed a crime more than half a century ago."
News of a re-trial was greeted with relief by the relatives of the people killed in the massacre. Newspapers said Italy must not squander this latest opportunity to confront its past.
"We expect a just sentence which once and for all will put an end to this terrible chapter of our recent history," La Stampa newspaper said in an editorial.
However some feared that Priebke, who lived openly for almost 50 years in Argentina before being brought to Italy for trial, could not now receive a fair hearing.
"They are doing all they can to make sure that Priebke dies in prison," said military judge Bruno Rocchi, who sat alongside Quistelli on the bench in the original trial.
